title: What has changed
hook: look at who you were on day one
tomorrow: the family finishes the whole book. what does Dadi do first?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the verse you kept: Musa in the shade, asking for whatever good God sends. One verse, kept. Today, a harder thing to look at: you.
screen: `ONE VERSE, KEPT.` → `NOW, A LOOK AT YOU.`

segments.voice: Every December the apps send a recap: your year in songs, in steps, in photos. This one arrives in person. A grandmother, home from knee surgery, leg up on a pillow, studies her granddaughter and says: you've changed. You pray on time now. You listen longer before you answer. And the granddaughter squirms. Part of her wants to say thank you. Part of her wants to say no, not really. So which is it? Should you count your own progress, or is counting your own good a trap?
screen: `YOUR YEAR IN REVIEW.` → `YOU'VE CHANGED.` → `COUNT IT, OR NOT?`

segments.voice: Both answers live inside the tradition. First, the case for looking. The Qur'an says change is real, and starts inside: God does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And a hadith in Tirmidhi says that whoever is glad at their good deed and sad at their bad one is a believer. Gladness at your good isn't pride; it's a sign of a living heart. The Qur'an even tells the Prophet ﷺ, after reminding him how far he's come: "Therefore of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse." Speak of the gift. Look back, see what's different, and say whose gift it was. Now the case for caution. The Qur'an also says: don't claim purity for yourselves; God knows best who is truly mindful of Him. Scholars name a quiet danger, 'ujb, admiring yourself, the good deed that turns into a mirror. And the Prophet said deeds are judged by how they end. A summit isn't a finish line. Someone who stops to admire the view can forget there's a way down, and a next climb. Here's what both sides share, and it's worth telling a friend tonight: neither says you haven't changed. They disagree about where to put your eyes. One says look at the gift and say thank you. The other says look at the road still ahead. A grandmother on a couch can hold both.
screen: `THE CASE FOR LOOKING.` · `GLAD AT YOUR GOOD.` · `THE CASE FOR CAUTION.` · `DEEDS ARE BY THEIR ENDINGS.` · then, large: `WHO I AM NOW.`

segments.voice: Take a scrap of paper and write one sentence: one thing that's different about you since you started this path. Under it, write who or what helped it change. Then turn the paper over and sit with the blank side until the time is up: that's the part still being written.
screen: `ONE CHANGE, ONE SENTENCE.` · `WHO HELPED IT HAPPEN.` · `THE BLANK SIDE.`

segments.voice: What has changed: the honest look back, held with thanks for the gift and an eye on the road ahead.
Your line: who I am now, given, and not finished. Twelve of fifteen, three to go.

screen: `DAY 1788 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 12 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: THEY FINISH THE WHOLE BOOK. WHAT DOES DADI DO FIRST?`

howItsDone: Muslims practice muhasaba, taking account of oneself, often at night or at the year's turn: thanking God for good that has grown and asking forgiveness for what hasn't, while scholars warn against self-admiration ('ujb).

fork.setup: your friend writes down every good deed each night and adds a gold star. a cousin calls it risky. give the cautious side's best case.
options: the Qur'an says don't claim purity for yourselves; God knows best who is mindful.
good deeds should be hidden even from the angels who record them.
writing things down is a modern habit, so it can't belong to faith.
fork.reveal: 53:32 and the warning against 'ujb are the cautious side's strongest ground. the other side has 13:11 and Tirmidhi 2165: being glad at your good is a sign of faith.

original.note: Arabic: the self, the soul; 13:11 speaks of what is 'in themselves' (bi-anfusihim).

trapdoor: what you thought: noticing your own progress is pride.
what it means: the tradition holds both: be glad and give thanks, and watch for self-admiration, since deeds are judged by their endings.
what a scholar hears: 13:11; Tirmidhi 2165; 93:11 'speak of the bounty'; 53:32; 'ujb in the books of the heart; Bukhari 6607 'deeds are by their endings'.
guess: an honest look at how you've grown
a list of the rules you've broken
proof that you've reached the end

chat.says: dadi's home, leg up, says i've changed. 'you pray on time now.' feels weird to agree. is that pride?
options: Not if you thank God for it. Just don't call it finished.
Yes, it's pride. Deny any change so you stay humble.
No, you earned it yourself, so go ahead and take the credit.
chat.meaning: Being glad at your good is a sign of faith (Tirmidhi 2165), and the Qur'an warns against claiming purity (53:32). Thank God, and keep going.

'ujb.meaning: self-admiration: a good deed that turns into a mirror

Tirmidhi.meaning: a major collection of hadith, by Imam al-Tirmidhi

Bounty.meaning: God's gifts; 93:11 says to speak of them

sources.quoted: Therefore of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse.

sources.ref: Qur'an 13:11 (God does not change a people's condition until they change what is in themselves)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2165 (whoever is glad at his good deed and sad at his bad deed is a believer)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6607 (deeds are judged by their endings)

notes: Debate day: 'look and give thanks' (13:11, Tirmidhi 2165, 93:11) and 'be wary of self-admiration' (53:32, 'ujb, Bukhari 6607), each in its strongest form; ranking neither.
93:11 is addressed to the Prophet; the voice says so. Applying it to the listener is a common devotional reading; confirm.
The 'gold star' in the fork is a new situation, not a ruling on journaling.
Gloss 'Bounty' glosses the English word in the quoted verse with the Arabic ni'ma; confirm that ni'ma is the word in 93:11 (bi-ni'mati rabbika).
